cells.tense: You are reading the whole shape clearly enough to catch when one part sits slightly off.
cells.act: clear the space the ending leaves
cells.ask: One arrangement here has already finished. Say its name to yourself once, then close it in the plainest way you have — a line on a page, a date taken down. You aren't deciding anything; you're freeing the room it was using.
cells.core:
You can step back far enough to see the whole shape of a thing, and from there the proportions are mostly right. When someone oversteps, you catch it. When someone carries more than their part, you catch that too. It doesn't sit heavy, because it isn't a tally running underneath — it's just what you see when you look.

That is what keeps the exchange moving here. What this balance is free to feed next is an ending: something in the arrangement has already finished, and letting it close is what frees the space for whatever comes after. Name the thing that's over, then close it in the simplest way — a line on a page, a date taken down, a quiet word that finishes it.
cells.sheetLine: You see the whole shape, so an ending here reads as clear.
cells.place: standing far enough back to see the whole shape of it

cells.tense: You will be tallying what each person owes the moment this lands in front of you.
cells.act: bear the next hour of it without deciding anything
cells.ask: Take the next hour of ordinary contact — the group thread, the meal, the meeting. Carry it without settling a single account in your head. When the urge to add it up arrives, wait until the hour is over before judging whether anything needs fixing.
cells.core:
Reading the whole shape is something you do well — you see who did what. What's ahead of you is the moment you'll want to reach for the scale. Something already out of proportion will come up, and the plan forms before it has landed: who's ahead, who's behind, what you'll say to even it.

For the next hour of ordinary contact, hold the shape without weighing it. Keep your own frame under the weight of what you see, and don't decide anything yet. If an imbalance is real, it will still be there later and you'll see it better. If it wasn't real, you've saved yourself the accounting. Holding isn't the same as ignoring — it's finishing the hour before you reach for the scale at all.
cells.sheetLine: Catch yourself adding it up and finish the hour first.
cells.place: standing far enough back to see the whole shape of it

cells.tense: You have been giving past your share for a long while, and you are still standing at that door.
cells.act: do the small practice again, alone, today
cells.ask: Seeing the imbalance and saying nothing is familiar ground. Today, keep a practice of your own — fifteen minutes on something you've been meaning to get to — and hold it through the days it feels pointless. Alone, no audience, nobody owed.
cells.core:
Stepping back to see the whole shape is something you do well, and what you see is your own side of it running short. You give past what's owed more often than not, because asking has stopped being something you reach for. The taking side isn't empty because you have nothing; it's empty because you stopped asking.

What the exchange needs from you is a practice of your own — the kind kept by attention and nothing else. Pick something you do alone, do it again today, and hold it through the days it feels pointless. Nothing is being demanded and nobody has to see it. Do the plain version first, before any plan for it.
cells.sheetLine: You see it uneven and stay quiet — begin there, not with a claim.

cells.tense: You are already keeping score in a room you did not know you were writing in.
cells.act: notice what you already know before you reason about it
cells.ask: There's a specific person you've been quietly counting things against, and you'd say there's nothing to it. Before you see them next, notice what you already knew about the score before your reasons arrived. Don't settle it. Just catch that you've been keeping it.
cells.core:
The whole shape is right there, and mostly you read it the open way — what's true across the room. Somewhere in it a narrower reading is running without your hand on it. Someone keeps coming up short, and a tally is being kept that you did not sit down to keep. If asked, you'd say you're fine with them. The tally says something else, quietly.

You don't have to confront anyone or settle anything. The next time you're near them, notice what you already knew about the score before the reasons got there. Let that first knowing land without arguing it back. That's the whole act — not deciding what the tally means, only knowing that your hand is the one holding the pen.
cells.sheetLine: The tally is real and yours — you didn't know you were keeping it.
cells.place: standing far enough back to see the whole shape of it
